title: History of Music & Instruments
subtitle: Grouped by what vibrates — which makes it physics.
objectives: Place the main stages of instrument history
Name Filipino instruments in each family
Explain what changes a note's pitch

cards.title: Instruments are grouped by what shakes
cards.text: Not by what they look like, and not by how loud they are. By which part of the instrument actually vibrates — which makes this a physics question.

cards.title: Five families, one test
cards.text: Ask one thing: what is moving back and forth fast enough to make sound?
points: **A string** — chordophone.
**A column of air** — aerophone.
**A stretched skin** — membranophone.
**The whole body of the thing** — idiophone.

cards.title: Five buttons
cards.text: Tap each family. The Filipino example is the one worth remembering.

question.text: A kulintang gong belongs to which family?
question.explain: Nothing is stretched over it. The bronze itself rings.

cards.title: Four moments, not four dates
cards.text: Each one solved a problem the one before it could not.
points: **About 40,000 years ago:** bone flutes, already with finger holes.
**Ancient civilisations:** harps, lyres, large drums, bronze gongs.
**From the 1600s:** the violin family and the keyboard, built to blend.
**From the 1900s:** electricity, and an instrument with no vibrating part.

cards.title: Pitch is a frequency, not a feeling
cards.text: High and low are not opinions. They are counts per second.
points: **Faster vibration = higher note.** That is the whole rule.
**Shorter string** vibrates faster. So does a tighter one.
**Shorter air column** vibrates faster.
**Smaller, thinner gong** vibrates faster. Same rule, four instruments.

question.text: You want a higher note from a guitar string. You should…
question.explain: Shorter means faster vibration, which means higher pitch.

cards.title: A speaker is an instrument built backwards
cards.text: An instrument turns movement into sound. A speaker turns a signal into movement.
points: **A coil of wire** sits inside a magnet.
**Current through the coil** makes it push and pull.
**The cone glued to it** moves the air.
**Same physics as a drum skin.** Different reason for moving.

cards.title: Game music has to not know what happens next
cards.text: A film score knows the running time. A game score does not.
points: **The music is written in layers.**
**Layers are added** as the danger rises.
**It loops without a seam** so you never hear it restart.
**That is a composing problem** no orchestra ever had.

terms.def: An instrument whose air column vibrates.
An instrument whose own body vibrates.
How high or low a note is — its vibration frequency.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Ask what vibrates: string, air, skin, body, or a circuit.
Kudyapi is a chordophone; tongali an aerophone; gangsa an idiophone.
Faster vibration means higher pitch, in every family.
Bone flutes with finger holes are about 40,000 years old.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 1 MAPEH, Music strand. The organising move is to drop the usual grouping by appearance and use the Hornbostel-Sachs question instead: what vibrates? That turns a memory task into a physics one, and it pays off immediately — the single rule that faster vibration means higher pitch then explains shortening a string, shortening an air column and choosing a smaller gong, all at once. Filipino instruments carry each family rather than appearing as a separate 'local' section. The history is given as four problems solved rather than four dates.
discussion: Ask what vibrates in each instrument in the house.
Ask why a smaller gong sounds higher.
Ask what a speaker and a drum have in common.
Ask how game music differs from film music.
extension: Have him find the highest and lowest note on one string and explain why.
Have him listen to a game soundtrack and count the layers.
misconceptions: "Instruments are grouped by size." By what vibrates.
"A gong is a drum." Nothing is stretched over a gong.
"Loose strings sound higher." Tighter is higher.
